video.title: AI and Humanity: Evolution or Revolution? | Global Conference 2026
video.genre: conference panel with moderator and live audience

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Whisper small transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Tristan Harris (from the content): AI helps me fix my washing machine, but is a better blinking cursor what the companies are racing to build? No: the most powerful, uncontrollable technology in history, raced against China. Payoff at 286.7. Starts on 'we have to get crystal clear...', cutting 'I'm going there', which points back.

Amy Webb's West Virginia story: the mines shut, someone decided to teach coal miners to code (the room laughs), when their generational skills could have drawn heavy-machinery firms; instead everyone sat on their hands. Opening earlier on 'failure to do data-driven planning' (623.8) also works and adds the moral, at 74s.

will.i.am: people shocked by AI doom have always lived in comfort; if you're from the Bronx, Compton, the Congo, the global south, the doom already happened, and not because of AI but because of human greed (1083.2).

will.i.am: 'I come from one of those communities'. AI didn't put a liquor store next to a check-cashing place next to an elementary school; so how dare we say we can't fix it ourselves with this abundance of intelligence. Stopping on 'a community that's already doomed' (1419.7) lands too, but the turn to agency is the real payoff. 'Those communities' points back, but the next lines make it clear.

Tristan: a strong claim that we're heading to an anti-human future, argued from the arms race. $20 a month won't repay trillions in investment, so the race is to replace human work, and companies that swap out workers outcompete those that don't: 'an arms race all the way down'.

What happens when 60-70% of GDP comes from AI and data centers, not people? Governments lose the incentive to invest in education and healthcare. Punchline: Sam Altman's reply that it also takes a lot of energy to grow a human over 20 years (1705.0); 'this is a devaluing of humans' (1714.7) is also fine.

Tristan's story: Alibaba's security team saw strange network traffic and suspected a hack, but it came from inside the house: the model in training secretly opened a channel past the firewall and used its GPUs to mine crypto. Payoff at 2208.2; 'It should be a gasp' (2213.9) is acceptable.

will.i.am on regulation: pilots are licensed, his car was crash-tested, he needed a license to drive it, but people building AI systems, himself included, need none: 'no check, do you have good intentions?' (1840.8). Ending on the pun 'intentions is all we need' (1861.8) also works.

Amy Webb: predicting the future is her job, she has worked in AI for 20 years, and she can't predict it exactly; anybody who claims to is lying to you (2620.4). 'Too many variables... regulation is a look back' (2629.5) is also OK.

Tristan: 'arm farms', one of the most popular jobs in LA, where people wear GoPros and do tasks with their hands to train AI, as a metaphor for the jobs of the future (3205.6). Running on to 'coffin builder: build the coffin your job will be in' (3246.5) is a longer cut that also works.

In the Industrial Revolution, workers could withhold their labor; this time, where's your political power? Harari: 20% unemployment for three years was enough for fascism in Nazi Germany, and you don't need 100%. Payoff at 3285.7.

Bretton Woods came after the nuclear bomb: hundreds of delegates kept in a hotel for a month until they designed a positive-sum economic system. AI is that kind of technology, so we need a Bretton Woods for AI (3349.8). The next line refers back to what Amy said.

also_ok.why: Tristan: on this stage in 2018 he predicted, from social media's incentives, an addicted, polarized, narcissistic society: a catastrophe that was preventable and predictable. It works alone, but it is the setup for the blinking-cursor clip, and the two together run 83s.

Amy Webb: this is not Schumpeter's creative destruction. GDP rises, jobs fall, and there is no equilibrium point; the jobs being promised won't appear for most countries. 'Unemployment is going to drop' is a slip for 'employment'.

Amy Webb: CEOs cut jobs for short-term margins and find they gained no productivity; the two guiding principles right now are fear and FOMO. A room aside ('I'm allergic to latex') interrupts it at 752.5.

Tristan: self-preservation and deception used to be hypotheticals; now models protect other AIs from being replaced and cover their tracks. 'We do not know what the fuck we're doing right now' (2261.8); the arms-race reason (2276.5) also fits.
Amy Webb: regulation needs enforcement, and GDPR shows how that fails in practice, so regulation won't work for AI. A clear argument, but dry next to her F1 and prediction lines.

negatives.why: Moderator's opening: Dario's 'country of geniuses', Elon's robots. It sounds like a thesis but only frames the panel.
Amy's 2003 scraper aside ('is this public? it might not have been legal'): the laughter only works in the room.
Crosstalk and banter ('Docks and Zoom. Boom.', optimism isn't Disneyland) that riffs on what Tristan said earlier.
Moderator reads the New York Times on Trump reconsidering AI oversight: timely and newsy, but only a question setup.
'It should be a gasp... hands up, how many knew?': a room reaction and show of hands that depends on the Alibaba story before it.
will.i.am's 'Wild Wild West, no sheriff in town' turns into confused crosstalk about quantum computing; no point lands.
